subtopic_detail: man in his late fifties with new disinhibition and loss of empathy referred as late onset bipolar disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 58-year-old builder referred by his general practitioner with a question of late onset bipolar disorder. Over the past two years his wife has watched him change from a considerate man into someone who makes crude remarks to strangers, laughed when their neighbour described her husband's cancer diagnosis, and was formally warned at work for walking off a job site mid shift.

He now eats several packets of biscuits daily, has gained 12 kg, and insists on the same lunch at the same cafe at the same time each day and becomes agitated if this is disrupted. His wife says he is not elated, does not need less sleep and talks no faster than usual. He is unbothered by any of it and says his wife worries too much. His father developed a similar change at 60 and died in a nursing home at 66. On testing he scores 27 out of 30 on a standardised cognitive screen with intact orientation and recall, but he names only five animals in a minute and continues an incorrect response pattern after being corrected.

data_table.Mental state: No elevated or expansive mood, no pressured speech, no reduced sleep need, marked lack of concern about his situation
data_table.Behavioural change: Disinhibition, loss of empathy, carbohydrate craving with 12 kg weight gain, rigid daily routines
data_table.Cognitive testing: Standardised screen 27 out of 30 with intact orientation and delayed recall, verbal fluency five animals in one minute, perseverative errors
data_table.Family history: Father with a similar behavioural change from age 60, died at 66

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for couples therapy addressing the relationship strain and review his progress in two months
options.rationale: Relationship intervention treats a psychosocial cause of behavioural change and carer strain is certainly present and worth supporting. Attributing an organic frontal syndrome to relationship difficulty places the responsibility on a man who cannot modify his behaviour. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence sodium valproate as a mood stabiliser and arrange psychiatric review in four weeks
options.rationale: Mood stabilisation treats the mania that this presentation superficially resembles, which is why the referral was framed that way. Mania requires elevated or irritable mood with reduced sleep need and pressured speech, and the two year progressive course without any mood elevation excludes it. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging and refer for formal neuropsychological assessment
options.rationale: Progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, hyperorality and compulsive routines with preserved memory and orientation but impaired verbal fluency and perseveration is behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia. Imaging for frontal and anterior temporal atrophy plus neuropsychology is the diagnostic pathway. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Request thyroid function with syphilis serology and a urine drug screen before any referral
options.rationale: Reversible causes deserve exclusion in any new neuropsychiatric presentation and these tests are part of a standard workup. They do not account for a two year progressive frontal syndrome with a matching family history, and relying on them alone delays the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence donepezil for a neurodegenerative process and arrange memory clinic review in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are for Alzheimer disease, the near pair, which presents with early episodic memory loss and preserved social conduct rather than the reverse pattern seen here. In frontotemporal dementia they are ineffective and can worsen behavioural symptoms. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the commonest cause of dementia under the age of sixty alongside Alzheimer disease and is routinely misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder for two to three years before the correct diagnosis is reached. The diagnostic criteria require three of six features: early behavioural disinhibition, apathy or inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality and dietary change, and a dysexecutive neuropsychological profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function. The pattern of preserved orientation and recall alongside markedly reduced verbal fluency and perseveration is characteristic and is what a bedside screen such as a standardised cognitive test will miss, since those instruments are weighted towards memory. A family history is present in up to 40 per cent, with mutations in the C9orf72, MAPT and GRN genes accounting for most inherited cases. There is no disease modifying treatment, so the value of early diagnosis lies in behavioural management, carer support, decisions about work and driving, and access to younger onset dementia services and financial planning.
key_points: Personality and conduct change with preserved memory is the reverse of Alzheimer disease.
Disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, hyperorality and dysexecutive testing.
Standard cognitive screens are insensitive because they weight memory and orientation.
A family history is present in up to 40 per cent of cases.
Cholinesterase inhibitors are ineffective and may worsen behaviour in this condition.
explanation.pearls: Verbal fluency is the single most useful bedside test when frontotemporal dementia is suspected: naming fewer than eleven animals in a minute is abnormal, and the discrepancy between a near normal memory score and a poor fluency score is what separates it from Alzheimer disease at first assessment.

subtopic_detail: older woman who became confused and unsteady three weeks after her antidepressant was started
stem:
You are the general practitioner called to see a 79-year-old woman at home by her son. Three weeks ago you started her on sertraline for a depressive episode and she had begun to sleep and eat a little better. Over the past four days she has become vague and muddled, has been unsteady on her feet with two near falls, and vomited twice yesterday.

She has hypertension treated with indapamide, which she has taken for six years, and no other medical history. She has not had diarrhoea, fever, cough or dysuria, and there has been no change to her fluid intake. On examination she is drowsy but rousable and oriented to person only, with moist mucous membranes, no postural drop in blood pressure, jugular venous pressure not elevated and no peripheral oedema. Chest is clear and the abdomen is soft. Sodium is 118 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45 to 90), serum osmolality 248 mmol/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg and urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Thyroid function and a morning cortisol are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only, moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no oedema, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45 to 90), serum osmolality 248 mmol/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L
data_table.Additional: Thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits, medications sertraline for three weeks and indapamide for six years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the sertraline, arrange hospital admission and commence careful fluid restriction
options.rationale: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with a low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the sertraline started three weeks ago is the new variable. Withdrawal of the drug with fluid restriction under inpatient monitoring is the correct combination at this sodium and conscious level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the indapamide, arrange hospital admission and commence intravenous normal saline
options.rationale: Thiazide and thiazide like diuretics are a leading cause of hyponatraemia in older people and indapamide should certainly also be stopped, so half of this is right. It has been taken unchanged for six years while the sertraline is new, and saline in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis can lower the sodium further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange admission for computed tomography of the brain and an intravenous fluid challenge
options.rationale: A fluid challenge is the right test when hypovolaemia is the suspected mechanism, but she has moist membranes, no postural drop and a urine sodium of 52 mmol/L, all of which indicate euvolaemia. Imaging investigates a structural cause for confusion that her electrolytes already explain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch her to mirtazapine at an equivalent dose and repeat the electrolytes in one week
options.rationale: Mirtazapine carries a lower risk of hyponatraemia and is a sensible choice when her depression is retreated later, so the drug selection itself is defensible. Substituting one antidepressant for another without treating a sodium of 118 mmol/L leaves the acute danger unaddressed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue current medications, restrict fluids to one litre daily and repeat electrolytes in two days
options.rationale: Outpatient fluid restriction with repeat testing is reasonable for mild asymptomatic hyponatraemia in a well patient. A sodium of 118 mmol/L with drowsiness, disorientation and vomiting is severe symptomatic hyponatraemia and carries a risk of seizure and cerebral oedema. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Antidepressant associated hyponatraemia through the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis is a common and under recognised adverse effect, with the highest risk in the first two to four weeks of treatment and in people over 65, of low body weight, or taking diuretics. All selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors carry the risk and venlafaxine and mirtazapine carry it to a lesser degree. The biochemical diagnosis requires hypotonic hyponatraemia with a serum osmolality below 275 mmol/kg, an inappropriately concentrated urine above 100 mmol/kg, a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, clinical euvolaemia, and the exclusion of hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. Severity is driven by symptoms and by rate of fall rather than by the absolute number, and drowsiness, vomiting and confusion at 118 mmol/L constitute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia requiring inpatient management. The correction rate must not exceed 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours because of the risk of osmotic demyelination, and a baseline sodium should be checked before starting an antidepressant in an older person and repeated at two weeks.
key_points: Risk is highest in the first two to four weeks and in older, lighter, diuretic treated patients.
Diagnosis requires hypotonic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L.
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before attributing it to the drug.
Saline can worsen the sodium in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis.
Do not correct faster than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours because of osmotic demyelination risk.
explanation.pearls: Check a baseline sodium before starting an antidepressant in anyone over 65 and repeat it at two weeks, because the median time to symptomatic hyponatraemia is around 13 days and the presentation is usually non specific confusion or a fall rather than anything that points to the electrolyte.

subtopic_detail: man with a drooping face who cannot raise the eyebrow on the affected side and cannot close that eye
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42-year-old carpenter who woke yesterday morning with the right side of his face not working. He noticed coffee dribbling from the corner of his mouth and his wife said his face looked crooked. He had noticed some pain behind the right ear the day before.

He says sounds seem uncomfortably loud in the right ear and that food tastes odd. He has had no fever, no rash, no headache, no limb weakness and no difficulty speaking or swallowing. He has not travelled outside Australia and has no tick exposure. On examination the right side of the face is weak throughout: he cannot wrinkle the right forehead, cannot fully close the right eye, and the right nasolabial fold is flattened. Power and reflexes are normal in all four limbs, the pupils are equal and reactive and eye movements are full. The external auditory canal and the tympanic membrane are normal with no vesicles, and the parotid region is normal on palpation.

data_table.Cranial nerves: Complete right sided facial weakness including the forehead, incomplete eye closure, hyperacusis and altered taste on the right
data_table.Neurological: Normal power, tone and reflexes in all four limbs, full eye movements, equal reactive pupils, normal speech and swallow
data_table.Ear and parotid: Normal external auditory canal and tympanic membrane with no vesicles, normal parotid on palpation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange serological testing for Lyme disease and defer treatment until the results return
options.rationale: Bilateral or sequential facial palsy with a preceding rash and overseas tick exposure would justify this, but there is no locally acquired Lyme disease in Australia. Waiting for serology would also take him past the window in which steroid works. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain and refer him to the stroke service today
options.rationale: Urgent stroke assessment is the correct response to an upper motor neurone facial weakness, the critical near pair, in which the forehead is spared because it receives bilateral cortical innervation. Complete forehead involvement localises the lesion to the nerve rather than the cortex. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Commence oral valaciclovir alone today and arrange review of his recovery in one week
options.rationale: Antiviral monotherapy is inferior to corticosteroid and is not recommended on its own. Adding an antiviral to prednisolone may give a small additional benefit in severe or complete palsy, but it never substitutes for the steroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone today and prescribe lubricating drops with overnight eye taping
options.rationale: Forehead involvement establishes a lower motor neurone facial palsy, and with a normal ear and no other cranial nerve signs this is Bell palsy. Corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset significantly improves the chance of complete recovery, and eye protection prevents exposure keratopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for facial nerve electrophysiological studies before deciding on any drug treatment
options.rationale: Electroneuronography has a role in prognostication for complete palsies that fail to recover, and it is occasionally used to guide decompression decisions. It has no place in the acute phase and delaying treatment for it costs the therapeutic window. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Bell palsy)

explanation.summary: Bell palsy is an acute idiopathic lower motor neurone facial palsy that evolves over hours to three days and accounts for most cases of unilateral facial weakness. The single most important examination step is testing the forehead, because the frontalis receives bilateral cortical input and is therefore spared in an upper motor neurone lesion such as a stroke but involved in a peripheral nerve lesion. Associated features that support a peripheral lesion include hyperacusis from stapedius weakness, altered taste over the anterior two thirds of the tongue from chorda tympani involvement, and postauricular pain. Corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset improves the probability of complete recovery from roughly 80 to over 90 per cent, and the evidence for adding an antiviral is weaker and limited to severe cases. Features that should prompt reassessment include bilateral palsy, other cranial nerve involvement, vesicles in the ear canal indicating Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a parotid mass, and failure to show any recovery by three weeks.
key_points: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neurone lesion and demands urgent stroke assessment.
Hyperacusis, altered taste and postauricular pain support a peripheral facial nerve lesion.
Corticosteroid within 72 hours substantially improves complete recovery rates.
Antivirals are adjunctive at best and never used alone.
Eye protection prevents exposure keratopathy and is part of every prescription.
explanation.pearls: Inspect the external auditory canal, the concha and the palate in every facial palsy, because the vesicles of Ramsay Hunt syndrome change the treatment to combined corticosteroid and antiviral therapy and carry a considerably worse prognosis for complete recovery.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

subtopic_detail: acutely hot swollen first toe joint in a man whose kidney function is severely reduced
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 66-year-old man who woke at 3 am with an exquisitely painful right great toe. He cannot bear the weight of the bedsheet on it. He has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each resolving over a week.

He has stage 4 chronic kidney disease from long standing hypertension and takes perindopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. He is not on a diuretic and takes no anticoagulant. He has no history of peptic ulcer disease, diabetes or heart failure. On examination he is afebrile and systemically well. The right first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, hot, swollen and exquisitely tender with overlying shiny skin, and there is no break in the skin and no ascending erythema or lymphangitis. No other joint is involved. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 24 mL/min/1.73 square metres, creatinine 248 micromol/L (60 to 110), serum urate 0.54 mmol/L (0.20 to 0.42), C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5) and white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Examination: Red hot swollen exquisitely tender right first metatarsophalangeal joint with shiny overlying skin, intact skin, no lymphangitis, no other joint involved
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 24 mL/min/1.73 square metres, creatinine 248 micromol/L (60 to 110), serum urate 0.54 mmol/L (0.20 to 0.42)
data_table.Additional: C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), medications perindopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for this acute episode?

options.text: A short course of oral prednisolone with review of his symptoms after five days
options.rationale: Severe renal impairment makes non steroidal agents hazardous and requires substantial colchicine dose reduction, so a short oral corticosteroid course is the preferred option for an acute flare in stage 4 chronic kidney disease. It is effective within 24 to 48 hours in a man with no diabetes or heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: A short course of oral indometacin with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line for acute gout in most patients and gastric protection addresses one of their risks. They can precipitate a further fall in glomerular filtration rate and hyperkalaemia at this level of renal function, particularly alongside an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence allopurinol at a low dose and titrate it upwards against the serum urate level
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy is the correct long term treatment after three attacks and with chronic kidney disease, and it should be started once things settle. Introducing it during an acute flare can prolong or worsen the attack unless anti inflammatory cover is already running. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Oral colchicine at the standard loading and maintenance dose used for an acute attack
options.rationale: Colchicine is genuinely useful in this situation but only at a substantially reduced dose, because it is renally cleared and accumulates. Standard dosing at an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24 risks myelosuppression and neuromyopathy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin for seven days with elevation of the limb and review in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Antibiotic therapy treats cellulitis, the near pair, which spreads diffusely beyond the joint margins with a portal of entry or lymphangitis and does not confine itself precisely to one joint. Erythema sharply limited to the joint with an intact skin surface is inflammatory rather than infective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute gout in chronic kidney disease is a common therapeutic bind because the two agents usually reached for first are both problematic. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs reduce renal perfusion through prostaglandin inhibition and can cause a further decline in function and hyperkalaemia, especially alongside renin angiotensin blockade, and are generally avoided below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 30. Colchicine is renally cleared, so dosing must be reduced substantially and it is avoided altogether in severe impairment or dialysis. That leaves corticosteroid as the pragmatic first choice for most patients with advanced kidney disease, given orally for a short course or injected intra articularly when a single large joint is involved and septic arthritis has been excluded. Once the flare settles, urate lowering therapy is indicated after recurrent attacks or with chronic kidney disease, starting allopurinol at a low dose appropriate to renal function and titrating to a target serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L.
key_points: Avoid non steroidal agents below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 30.
Colchicine is renally cleared and needs substantial dose reduction or avoidance.
Corticosteroid is the pragmatic first choice in advanced chronic kidney disease.
Aspirate the joint whenever fever, systemic upset or diagnostic doubt is present.
Start urate lowering therapy after the flare settles, targeting urate below 0.36 mmol/L.
explanation.pearls: Serum urate is frequently normal or low during an acute flare because urate shifts into the inflamed joint, so a normal level never excludes gout and the measurement that guides treatment is the one taken two to four weeks after the attack has settled.

subtopic_detail: older woman with an acutely swollen knee and a thin white line in the joint cartilage on radiograph
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman admitted yesterday for management of community acquired pneumonia, who has developed a painful swollen left knee overnight. She is on day two of intravenous benzylpenicillin and is improving from a respiratory point of view.

She has had no previous joint problems, no recent injury and no prosthetic joints. She takes no anticoagulant. On examination she is alert with a temperature of 37.8 degrees. The left knee is warm, swollen with a demonstrable effusion, and painful through the last 20 degrees of flexion, though she can straight leg raise. There is no overlying skin break, no rash and no other joint involvement. A plain radiograph of the knee shows a fine linear opacity within the meniscal cartilage and within the hyaline cartilage of both femoral condyles, with moderate joint space narrowing. C reactive protein is 88 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) and serum urate is 0.28 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.40).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees
data_table.Examination: Warm swollen left knee with demonstrable effusion, painful terminal flexion, able to straight leg raise, no skin break or rash
data_table.Imaging: Knee radiograph showing linear calcification within the meniscal and hyaline cartilage with moderate joint space narrowing
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), serum urate 0.28 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral colchicine at a reduced dose and reassess the knee again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Colchicine is used for crystal arthritis including calcium pyrophosphate disease and would be reasonable once infection has been excluded. Her normal serum urate does not exclude gout during an attack either, and neither crystal has yet been demonstrated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee to assess for osteomyelitis and a joint effusion
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is sensitive for bone marrow oedema and is useful when osteomyelitis is suspected or a joint cannot be accessed. It cannot distinguish crystal from infection in synovial fluid, which is the actual question, and it delays the answer by a day. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Inject the joint with corticosteroid after confirming the radiographic calcification is present
options.rationale: Intra articular corticosteroid is an excellent treatment for an acute calcium pyrophosphate flare in a single large joint and is what she is likely to need. Injecting steroid into an undiagnosed effusion in a febrile patient risks converting a treatable infection into a destroyed joint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Aspirate the joint and send fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal examination
options.rationale: Cartilage calcification makes calcium pyrophosphate arthritis likely but never excludes infection, and a febrile inpatient with a hot joint and a raised C reactive protein must have septic arthritis ruled out. Aspiration answers both questions from one sample and must precede any treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Broaden the antibiotic cover to intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange orthopaedic review today
options.rationale: Empirical antistaphylococcal cover is appropriate once septic arthritis is genuinely suspected, but treating before aspiration substantially reduces the yield of synovial culture. The organism is what determines the duration and the route of therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease produces chondrocalcinosis, the linear calcification of hyaline and fibrocartilage seen on plain films, and its acute inflammatory form was traditionally called pseudogout. The crucial management point is that radiographic chondrocalcinosis is common in the elderly and its presence never excludes septic arthritis, which in a native joint destroys cartilage within days and carries substantial mortality. Synovial fluid analysis is therefore mandatory, and a single aspirate gives the cell count, the Gram stain and culture, and the polarised light examination that identifies positively birefringent rhomboid crystals of calcium pyrophosphate or negatively birefringent needles of monosodium urate. Crystals and infection can coexist, so a positive crystal result does not close the question if the fluid also looks purulent or the cell count is very high. Once infection is excluded, treatment is intra articular corticosteroid for a single joint, or oral corticosteroid or colchicine where several joints are involved, and secondary causes including hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis and hypomagnesaemia are worth considering in younger patients.
key_points: Chondrocalcinosis is common in older people and never excludes septic arthritis.
Acute flares are often triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma.
One aspirate provides cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal analysis.
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent.
Aspirate before starting antibiotics to preserve the culture yield.
explanation.pearls: A synovial fluid white cell count above 50 x10^9 per litre with a neutrophil predominance points strongly to septic arthritis whatever crystals are also seen, and the two can genuinely coexist, so the crystal result never overrides a purulent aspirate.
